title: Bias and treating people fairly
blurb: Tell conscious from unconscious bias, see how bias shapes project decisions, and adapt your behaviour so everyone can contribute.
question: A project manager always gives the high-profile client presentations to Tom, who went to her university and shares her love of cycling, although Priya has more client experience. What kind of bias may be at work, and how should the project manager make the allocation fairer?

teach.h: Bias: the shortcut that skews judgement
teach.body: Bias is a tendency to favour or disfavour certain people or ideas, which can lead to unfair judgements. CONSCIOUS bias (explicit) is one we are aware of: a known preference or prejudice. UNCONSCIOUS bias (implicit) works without our awareness: mental shortcuts shaped by our background, culture and experience. Everyone has unconscious biases, including fair-minded people. In plain English: our brains take shortcuts, and some of them are unfair.

rows.label: Example
values: 'I won't put a parent on night shifts'
Warming to a candidate just like you

rows.label: Main remedy
values: Challenge it; policy and conduct rules

teach.caption: Both can lead to unfair treatment, and if a decision is based on a protected characteristic it may be unlawful discrimination.

teach.h: Taking bias out of a decision
teach.caption: Awareness training helps people notice bias; structured processes stop it deciding the outcome.

teach.body: Treating people fairly means giving everyone an equal chance to contribute, which often means ADAPTING your behaviour to individual needs. For disabled people, employers have a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010 to make reasonable adjustments that remove disadvantage. Good practice goes further: flexible working, respecting religious observance, inclusive meetings and adjusting your communication style. Treating everyone identically can itself be unfair if it leaves some people unable to take part.

head: Need
Adaptation
rows: Papers shared early, clear formats, verbal summary
Schedule around prayer times and festivals
teach.caption: Ask the person what helps. Don't assume: the individual is the expert on their own needs.

teach.text: Two classic traps. 1) Unconscious bias is NOT deliberate: it affects everyone, so 'I'm not biased' is no defence and process is the safeguard. 2) 'Treat everyone exactly the same' sounds fair but is the wrong answer when someone needs an adjustment to contribute.

teach.body: Grace realises Tom gets every client presentation because she feels a natural rapport with him (affinity bias), while Priya, with more client experience, is overlooked. She agrees criteria for presenters (client knowledge, relevant experience, development need), rotates the role and asks a colleague to sense-check allocations. In her iterative project she also uses simultaneous estimating so junior voices are not anchored by the most senior one.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define conscious bias (aware) and unconscious bias (not aware, mental shortcuts).
Name a specific bias (affinity, confirmation, halo) and the action it distorts.
Explain the effect: unfair decisions, lost talent, disengagement, possible discrimination.
Give fair-treatment measures: training, agreed criteria, diverse panels, inclusive meetings.
Show adapting behaviour: reasonable adjustments and flexible working so everyone contributes.
Conscious bias is known to us; unconscious bias works without our awareness.
Affinity, confirmation, halo and proximity bias skew recruitment, tasks, promotion and decisions.
Counter it with awareness, objective criteria, diverse panels and reviewing patterns.
Fair treatment means adapting to individual needs, not treating everyone identically.
Reasonable adjustments for disabled people are a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010.

summary: You can now distinguish conscious from unconscious bias, name the common biases and explain how they distort project actions. You can also describe practical ways to treat people fairly, including structured decisions, reasonable adjustments and adapting your own behaviour to individual needs.

A.q: Which statement best describes unconscious bias?
options: A deliberate decision to exclude a group of staff
Preferences that shape judgements without us knowing
An organisational policy that openly favours some staff
A formal, documented method of ranking candidates
A.why: Unconscious (implicit) bias is a set of mental shortcuts and preferences that influence our judgements without our awareness.

whyNot.0: A deliberate decision describes conscious (explicit) bias, not unconscious bias.
whyNot.2: An open policy is deliberate and visible, so it is not unconscious.
whyNot.3: A documented ranking method is a process, not a bias; structured methods actually help reduce bias.

A.q: An interviewer warms to a candidate because they grew up in the same town and share the same hobbies. Which bias is this?
A.why: Affinity bias is the tendency to favour people who are similar to us in background, interests or experience.

whyNot.0: Confirmation bias is seeking evidence that supports a view we already hold.
whyNot.1: The halo effect is letting one positive trait colour our whole judgement of someone.
whyNot.2: Proximity bias is favouring people who are physically near us, such as office-based staff.

A.q: Which action would best reduce bias when recruiting a new project team member?
options: Informal chats to see who fits in
A.why: Structured interviews with agreed, job-related criteria make candidates comparable on evidence, limiting the room for bias.

whyNot.1: 'Fit' judged informally is where affinity bias thrives.
whyNot.2: Relying on recommendations tends to recruit people like the existing team.
whyNot.3: A single decision-maker's biases go unchallenged; diverse panels are better.

B.q: A project manager rates a team member as excellent in every area of an appraisal, largely because of one outstanding client presentation. Which bias is this?
B.why: The halo effect is when one strong positive impression spreads to our judgement of everything else about a person.

whyNot.0: Affinity bias is about favouring people who are similar to us.
whyNot.1: Confirmation bias is filtering evidence to fit an existing view; here one trait colours the whole rating.
whyNot.3: The project manager isn't aware of the distortion, so it isn't conscious bias.

B.q: A team member with a hearing impairment struggles to follow fast-moving video calls. Which response best treats them fairly?
options: Treat them the same as all others
Move them to tasks with no meetings
Ask colleagues to summarise for them
B.why: Agreeing reasonable adjustments with the person (live captions, written notes) removes the disadvantage so they can contribute fully.

whyNot.0: Identical treatment leaves them at a disadvantage; fairness here means adapting.
whyNot.1: Removing them from meetings excludes them rather than supporting them.
whyNot.2: Relying on colleagues' summaries is a poor substitute and makes them dependent; ask what they need.

B.q: Which statement about treating people fairly is correct?
options: Fairness means everyone gets identical treatment
Fairness only applies to recruitment decisions
Fairness can mean adapting to individual needs
Adjustments only apply to those asking in writing
B.why: Fair treatment gives everyone an equal chance to contribute, which often means adapting behaviours and arrangements to individual needs.

whyNot.0: Identical treatment can be unfair if some people need adjustments to take part.
whyNot.1: Fairness applies to task allocation, meetings, development and promotion too.
whyNot.3: There is no rule that requests must be in writing; a good manager also notices and asks.

C.q: In a hybrid team, the project manager notices the most interesting tasks keep going to people who sit near her in the office. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask remote staff to come in more often
Allocate against criteria and check patterns
Accept that office staff are more reliable
Let the team pick tasks first-come first-served
C.why: This looks like proximity bias. Allocating work against agreed criteria and reviewing who gets what makes allocation fair whatever someone's location.

whyNot.0: This treats the symptom by pressuring remote staff rather than fixing the biased allocation.
whyNot.2: Assuming office staff are more reliable is the bias itself.
whyNot.3: First-come first-served favours whoever is online or nearby first, which can repeat the same pattern.

C.q: Having decided early that Supplier A is best, a project manager reads closely only the evidence that supports that view during evaluation. Which bias is this, and what is the best control?
options: Affinity bias: ask the supplier for references
Halo effect: shorten the evaluation period
Conscious bias: let the sponsor choose instead
C.why: Seeking evidence that confirms an existing view is confirmation bias. Pre-agreed criteria and weightings, scored by several people, force all the evidence to be considered.

whyNot.1: Affinity bias is favouring people like us, and more references wouldn't fix selective reading.
whyNot.2: The halo effect is one trait colouring the whole view; a shorter evaluation would make it worse.
whyNot.3: The PM isn't aware of it, so it isn't conscious bias, and passing the decision on doesn't remove bias.

C.q:
Which THREE actions help a project manager treat a global team fairly?
1. Rotating meeting times across time zones
2. Sharing papers before workshops
3. Giving key work to those most like the PM
4. Flexible hours for religious observance
C.why: Rotating meeting times, sharing papers in advance and flexing hours for observance all adapt to individual needs so everyone can contribute.

whyNot.0: Giving key work to people like the PM (3) is affinity bias.
whyNot.2: Includes affinity bias (3) and leaves out rotating meeting times (1).
whyNot.3: Includes affinity bias (3) and leaves out sharing papers in advance (2).

reteach.title: Marking a pile of school essays
reteach.question: A teacher must mark 30 essays, including one from a pupil she knows is a star student. How does she keep the marking fair, and what does 'fair' mean for a pupil with dyslexia?

blocks.body: If she sees the star pupil's name, she may mark generously before reading a word (the halo effect, an unconscious bias). So schools use blind marking, a marking scheme agreed in advance and a second marker. Fairness also means a pupil with dyslexia may get extra time in exams: adapting the arrangements so the test measures their knowledge, not their reading speed. Projects work the same way.

blocks.text: Extra time isn't an unfair advantage: it removes a disadvantage. That is exactly what a reasonable adjustment does at work.

explain.body: Conscious bias is a preference we know we hold and could voice. Unconscious bias is automatic, shaped by background and experience, and we don't notice it working. Both can make treatment unfair.

test.q: A manager openly says he prefers not to hire older applicants because they 'won't adapt to new tools'. This is an example of:
test.why: He is aware of and states his preference, so it is conscious (explicit) bias. Acting on it would also be age discrimination.

whyNot.1: Unconscious bias operates without awareness; he is stating his view openly.
whyNot.2: The halo effect is one positive trait colouring a whole judgement.
whyNot.3: Proximity bias is favouring people who are physically near us.

explain.body: Affinity bias favours people like us. Confirmation bias seeks evidence for what we already believe. The halo effect lets one good trait colour everything. Proximity bias favours people who are physically near us.

test.q: Which bias leads someone to favour information that supports what they already believe?
test.why: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice, seek and believe information that confirms our existing views.

whyNot.0: Affinity bias is favouring people similar to ourselves.
whyNot.1: The halo effect is one positive trait shaping our overall view of a person.
whyNot.2: Proximity bias is favouring people who are physically close to us.

explain.body: Because unconscious bias is invisible to the person who has it, the best safeguards are structural: criteria agreed in advance, diverse panels, independent scoring and checking outcomes for patterns. Awareness training helps people spot it.

test.q: Why do diverse selection panels help reduce bias?
options: Their mix of views checks any one bias
They remove the need for criteria
They let the sponsor overrule the PM
test.why: Panel members with different perspectives notice and challenge each other's biases, so no single person's shortcuts decide the outcome.

whyNot.0: Panels usually take longer; their value is fairness, not speed.
whyNot.2: Panels still need agreed criteria to score against.
whyNot.3: Panels are about balanced judgement, not about the sponsor's authority.

explain.body: Treating people fairly means removing barriers. For disabled people, the Equality Act 2010 requires employers to make reasonable adjustments. Beyond that, good managers flex meeting times, formats, working hours and their own communication style to individual needs.

test.q: Under the Equality Act 2010, employers have a legal duty to make reasonable adjustments for:
test.why: The legal duty to make reasonable adjustments applies to disabled people. Adapting for others (such as flexible hours for carers) is good practice and may be supported by other rights.

whyNot.0: Age alone does not trigger the duty to make reasonable adjustments.
whyNot.1: Anyone may ask, but the specific legal duty under the Act relates to disability.
whyNot.3: The duty is not limited to contractors; it covers disabled employees and job applicants.
